passage:
Ritu,
At the reunion you asked, "So what are you building these days?" and I laughed and said, "My loan repayment history." Everyone laughed. I've been thinking about it for a week.
Honest answer: nothing. I get to the office at 9:40, do the same reconciliations, eat the same paneer roll, watch two episodes and sleep. The salary is good. The flat is comfortable. Ma thinks her daughter has it all sorted. I'm not unhappy, exactly. I'm just flat. When you talked about your library project in the village, I felt something close to jealousy, and then nothing, which was worse.
I don't think I'm lazy. I work hard. It's just that everything I do comes back to me: my money, my comfort, my weekend. There's nobody else in it.
Can we talk on Saturday?
Kalyani

qa.q: What did Kalyani answer when Ritu asked what she was building?
qa.a: "My loan repayment history."

qa.q: What did Kalyani feel when Ritu talked about the library project?
qa.a: She felt something close to jealousy and then nothing, which worried her more because it showed how flat she had become.

qa.q: What first step does asking Ritu to talk on Saturday suggest?
qa.a: Naming the flatness to a friend is a first move outward; talking could help Kalyani find one thing to care about beyond her own comfort.

qa.q: How might Ritu feel reading this letter?
qa.a: Ritu may feel trusted and a little concerned, and glad Kalyani answered honestly instead of joking again.

grounding: A young worker with a comfortable routine feels flat when asked what she is building, realising her life points only at herself though she is not lazy.

passage: Kishore, you'll laugh, but your question at Diwali is still stuck in my head. "What are you building, Ujjwal?" I said, "A fixed deposit." Funny, right? But here's my week. Office at ten, the same three dashboards, lunch at my desk, gym at seven, food delivery, a series, sleep. Weekend: sleep more, the mall with my flatmates. My salary goes up every year. Ma calls me her comfortable son. And I am comfortable. I'm not lazy either; I clear every target. It's just that when you asked, I saw that every single thing on that list is about me. My body, my money, my screen. Nobody's life is different because I'm in it. The feeling isn't sad, exactly. It's more like a room with no windows. Anyway. Pass the biscuits.

qa.q: What did Ujjwal answer when Kishore asked what he was building?
qa.a: "A fixed deposit."

qa.q: What feeling is Ujjwal describing with "a room with no windows"?
qa.a: A closed-in flatness: comfortable but cut off, because everything in his life points back at himself.

qa.q: What could Ujjwal try as one small change?
qa.a: He could add one weekly thing that involves someone else, so at least part of his week reaches beyond himself.

qa.q: How might Kishore feel hearing this answer to a Diwali question?
qa.a: Kishore may be surprised that a passing question struck so deep, and want to help Ujjwal find a window 🤔

grounding: A young worker in a comfortable routine realises his whole life is turned inward and feels flat, though he works hard and is not lazy.

passage: I'm Jahnavi, Akash's older sister, and I've shared this flat with him for two years. From outside, his life looks fine. He leaves at 9:15, comes back at seven, orders the same biryani every Friday, and the salary slip he leaves on the table gets bigger each April. He isn't lazy; he has never missed a day. Last Sunday our cousin's six-year-old asked him, "What do you make at your job?" Akash opened his mouth, closed it and said, "Money." The kid lost interest. Akash didn't. He sat on the balcony for a long time without his phone, which he never does. I don't know what he was thinking. But on Monday he asked me, quite casually, what my weekend teaching class was like.

qa.q: What did Akash answer when asked what he makes at his job?
qa.a: "Money."

qa.q: What might Akash sitting on the balcony without his phone suggest?
qa.a: The question seems to have unsettled him, maybe leaving him feeling flat or wondering what he is really building, though Jahnavi can't be sure.

qa.q: What turning point does Akash's Monday question suggest, and how could Jahnavi help?
qa.a: It hints he is looking beyond his routine; Jahnavi could invite him to her teaching class once, with no pressure.

qa.q: How does Jahnavi see her brother's life?
qa.a: From outside it looks fine, steady and well paid, but she notices the sameness and the long quiet on the balcony.

grounding: A sister watches her brother's comfortable, inward routine and his flatness when a child asks what he makes, noting he is not lazy.

passage:
Monday. Anjali, twenty-five, reached the insurance office at 9:40, processed the same claim forms as always, ate lunch at her desk, and was home by half past six for an episode of her series and dal from the corner shop. It was comfortable. Her salary had gone up in April. She told herself that was enough.
Thursday. At a friend's housewarming, Joseph, from her college batch, talked about the evening literacy class he had started. Then he asked, "What are you building these days, Anjali?" She laughed. "My savings." On the way home it didn't feel funny. She felt flat, like a room with the windows shut.
Sunday. She tried to list things she had done last month that weren't for herself, and stopped at the empty page. She wasn't lazy; she worked hard. Everything just pointed inward. She left the notebook open on the table.

qa.q: What did Anjali answer when Joseph asked what she was building?
qa.a: She laughed and said, 'My savings.'

qa.q: Why did Anjali's joke stop feeling funny on the way home?
qa.a: She realised her life was comfortable but pointed only at herself, which left her feeling flat, like a room with the windows shut.

qa.q: What small step might Anjali take after staring at the empty page?
qa.a: She could ask Joseph about his literacy class, or choose one thing each week to do for someone else, opening a window outward.

qa.q: How might Joseph see Anjali's 'My savings' answer?
qa.a: He may take it as a joke without guessing how flat it left her, or he may sense something unsaid behind the laugh.

grounding: Over a week a hardworking young woman settled in comfort realises her life points only inward and feels flat when asked what she is building.

passage:
"Wasim, young man, you told me work is 'fine, just boring' and you only look forward to payday. Let your Devika Aunty from next door tell you about herself at twenty-five.
I was a clerk at the electricity office. Good salary, fixed hours, a new pressure cooker every Diwali, and every evening the radio and bed. I wasn't lazy. I was punctual; I never took a day off. But one evening my father asked, 'What are you building, Devika?' and I had nothing to say. I felt as flat as the ledger on my desk.
It took me two more years to notice that everything I did was for me: my comfort, my salary, my Sundays. A life folded in on itself.
I'm not telling you what to do. I'm only saying that if the question makes you feel flat too, it's worth listening to."

qa.q: Where did Devika Aunty work at twenty-five?
qa.a: She was a clerk at the electricity office.

qa.q: How did Devika feel when her father asked what she was building?
qa.a: She felt empty and flat, as flat as the ledger on her desk, because she had nothing to say.

qa.q: What does Devika suggest Wasim do with his own flat feeling?
qa.a: To listen to it as a sign rather than ignore it, since it took her two years to notice her life had folded inward.

qa.q: What might Devika's father have hoped she would see when he asked, 'What are you building, Devika?'
qa.a: He may have wanted her to look past the good salary and comfort and ask whether her days were adding up to anything.

grounding: An elder recalls being a punctual, comfortable young clerk whose life had turned entirely inward, and feeling flat when asked what she was building.
